tagline: Granite islands in the Indian Ocean
overview:
Seychelles is an archipelago of about 115 islands scattered across the Indian Ocean roughly 1,500 kilometers east of the African mainland. It is the smallest country in Africa by both land and population: all the islands together cover about 450 square kilometers, and only around 100,000 people live on them.

Most Seychellois live on Mahé, where the capital, Victoria, sits beneath forested peaks; Praslin and La Digue are the next largest islands. Three languages are official: Seychellois Creole, which nearly everyone speaks at home, plus English and French. Seychelles is a republic with an elected president.

The inner islands are unusual because they are made of granite, the remains of an ancient continent that split apart, rather than coral or volcanic rock like most ocean islands. Their boulder-strewn beaches, clear water, and rare wildlife draw visitors from around the world, and tourism and tuna fishing are the country's main industries.
landAndNature: The granite inner islands rise steeply from the sea, reaching 905 meters on Mahé, with huge weathered boulders piled along the shore. Farther out lie flat coral islands and atolls, including Aldabra, one of the largest coral atolls on Earth and home to roughly 100,000 giant tortoises, more than anywhere else in the world. The climate is warm and humid all year, with a rainy northwest monsoon and a drier, breezier southeast season. The Vallée de Mai on Praslin is a palm forest holding the coco de mer, whose nut is the heaviest seed of any plant. Black parrots, fairy terns, and hawksbill turtles live here among fringing coral reefs.
peopleAndCulture: Seychellois people descend from French settlers, enslaved Africans, and later Indian, Chinese, and British arrivals, and Creole culture blends all of it. Seychellois Creole grew out of French and has its own spelling system. Meals come from the sea and the garden: grilled fish with chili and lime, octopus curry in coconut milk, breadfruit, and mangoes. The moutya, a slow drum dance once performed by enslaved people at night and long discouraged by authorities, is now recognized by UNESCO, while the faster sega is danced at parties. Most Seychellois are Catholic. Fishing, sailing, and soccer fill free time, and the Creole Festival each October celebrates language, food, and music.
history: Seychelles had no permanent inhabitants until modern times, though Arab and other sailors probably passed by and Portuguese ships charted the islands in the 1500s. France claimed them in 1756 and brought settlers and enslaved Africans to grow spices, cotton, and coconuts. Britain took over in 1814 and abolished slavery in the 1830s; Africans freed from intercepted slave ships were landed here, adding to the population. Seychelles became independent on June 29, 1976. A coup the following year brought one-party rule that lasted until multiparty elections returned in 1993. The country is now known for protecting its environment, setting aside nearly half its land and a vast stretch of ocean as reserves.
funFacts: The coco de mer palm produces the heaviest seed in the world, weighing up to about 18 kilograms.
Aldabra atoll is home to far more giant tortoises than the whole country has people, roughly 100,000 of them.
Seychelles has no native land mammals except bats; nearly every other animal on land arrived by ship.
Jonathan, a Seychelles giant tortoise hatched around 1832 and now living on Saint Helena, is the oldest known land animal.
The inner islands are granite, a rock usually found on continents, left stranded when India drifted away millions of years ago.
